title: The greatest commandment (Mark 12:28–34)
hook: love God with all you are, and your neighbor as yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was resurrection, standing up again. Your line was god of the living.

After a string of traps, a different kind of person walks up. A scribe, an expert in the Law, has been listening at the edge of the crowd, and he's noticed that Jesus answered well. So he asks a real question, not a trick. In the King James Bible: "Which is the first commandment of all?" The Law of Moses is long, and full of commands. If you had to put a whole life's faith on one index card, what would go on it? Jesus doesn't need to think about it. He starts with a single word, straight from the book of Deuteronomy.
screen: `A SCRIBE, LISTENING.` → `A REAL QUESTION, NOT A TRAP.` → `WHICH IS THE FIRST?`

segments.voice: Here's his answer: "The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment." Hear, in Hebrew, is Shema. It's the first word of Deuteronomy chapter six, verse four, and the name of the prayer built around it. Deuteronomy itself says to talk of these words when you lie down and when you rise up, and to write them on the doorposts of your house. Jesus was a Jew, and asked for the heart of it all, he answers from his own people's scripture. He doesn't stop at one. He adds a second, from Leviticus: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two loves, side by side: love of God, and love of the person next to you. Then something rare in a chapter full of traps. The scribe agrees, warmly. Well said, teacher. Loving God and neighbor matters more than all the burnt offerings and sacrifices. And Jesus, seeing he answered wisely, says: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." After that, Mark says, nobody dared ask him anything more. One small detail: in Hebrew, Deuteronomy lists heart, soul and strength. Mark's version has four, adding mind. All of you, every part, nothing held back.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `THE PRAYER OF HIS PEOPLE.` · `LOVE GOD, AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `A SCRIBE WHO AGREES.` · then, large: `THOU ART NOT FAR FROM THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Say both commandments slowly, aloud or in your head, one phrase per breath: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord; love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, with all your strength; and love your neighbor as yourself. Then sit with whichever phrase caught you. If you don't pray, you can simply notice which of the two loves feels harder today.
Shema. Hebrew for hear, the first word of the prayer Jesus named as the first commandment of all.
Your line: not far from the kingdom. Two loves, one answer. Tomorrow, a widow at the treasury.

howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the two great commandments, and some churches read them aloud in worship as a summary of the Law; in Jewish prayer the Shema is said morning and evening, and Christians sometimes note that Jesus answered from it.

original.note: Hebrew: hear, listen. the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4 and the name of the prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shema is just a Hebrew word for listen.
what it means: the first word of Israel's central prayer, which Jesus names first of all, and pairs with love of neighbor.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 6:4–5 and Leviticus 19:18 joined; Mark keeps Hear, O Israel, and lists four, adding mind to heart, soul and strength.

chat.says: When someone asked Jesus for the most important commandment, what did he say?
options: Love God with all you are, and love your neighbor as yourself.
He said he couldn't choose, and told the scribe to go read the Law.
He named the temple sacrifices as the heart of the whole Law.
chat.meaning: Jesus answered with the Shema: love God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength. Then he added Leviticus: love your neighbor as yourself.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Cut the unsourced 613-commandments count, "teachers loved to ask", and "every Jewish child ... would have known by heart". "He very likely said the Shema morning and evening" and the mezuzah line replaced with what Deuteronomy 6:7 and 6:9 themselves say. "Never meant to be separated" and the superlative "the kindest exchange" softened; trapdoor's "only Mark keeps" removed.
613 commandments: a later rabbinic count (Talmud, Makkot 23b); the script says 'later Jewish tradition'. Confirm.

'He very likely said the Shema morning and evening': an inference (twice-daily recitation is attested in the Mishnah, later than Jesus); softened from 'would have said ... every morning and evening', and the screen line changed from 'THE PRAYER JESUS SAID DAILY' to 'THE PRAYER OF HIS PEOPLE'. Confirm.
Corrected 'the first word of Deuteronomy chapter six' to 'chapter six, verse four' (6:1 begins differently).
Mezuzah described as 'the small scroll many Jewish families fix to their doorposts'. Confirm.
Deuteronomy 6:5 Hebrew: levav, nefesh, me'od (heart, soul, might); Mark 12:30 has four terms. Matthew 22:37 omits 'Hear, O Israel' and the scribe's reply. Confirm.
Practice paraphrases the verses in modern words for recitation; the KJV is quoted in the teach.
